messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David is a 63-year-old rabbi who came to treatment after months of telling himself he should be able to handle this on his own. He had arrived in the United States as a child refugee after armed men forced their way into his family’s neighborhood, shouting orders in the street and striking people with whatever they carried. What remains most vivid to him is not a complete story but sharply preserved moments: the sight of weapons in men’s hands, the sound of voices suddenly raised, and the shock of being grabbed and pulled before he understood what was happening. Even now, he says his body reacts before his mind does, as if it still lives in that earlier world. In session he speaks quietly, but when he describes those moments he becomes visibly tense, as though the old danger is present again.

For years David built a life that looked steady from the outside. He became a rabbi, known for warmth and composure, and he now lives with a long-term partner who has grown increasingly aware of how narrow his sense of safety has become. The difficulties intensified over the last few years as the congregation became larger and more physically informal. During greetings after services, an unexpected hand on his shoulder can make him flinch hard enough to lose his train of thought. If a visitor enters wearing something at the belt that resembles a weapon, or if a disagreement in the social hall turns into shouting, he feels himself pulled out of the present. In those moments he immediately tries to push his attention somewhere else—onto the order of the prayer books, the agenda for a committee meeting, the coffee urn—anything to distract himself from the rush in his body. He also grows more distant afterward, withholding affection and emotional openness from his partner because closeness leaves him feeling too exposed.

These episodes do not feel random to David. Each time he startles, he takes it as evidence that something is wrong with him: his body, in his words, has become an enemy that refuses to understand when he is safe. He has come to believe he cannot rely on himself if danger appears, and he compares himself harshly to an imagined stronger person who would have stopped what happened long ago. The trigger and the meaning arrive almost together; the raised voice or sudden touch does not just frighten him, it confirms his conviction that he is fundamentally unsteady. Once he is thinking this way, the world seems easier to ignite. A hand reaching for a friendly embrace, a ceremonial object held too abruptly, even loud enthusiasm from congregants can register first as threat, because he is already braced for proof that he is not in control.

That belief has narrowed his daily life. David now scans rooms automatically and chooses his seat in every setting—sanctuary, restaurant, family gathering—according to where he feels most protected, usually near an exit or against a wall where no one can come up behind him. He notices where voices are rising before he can follow what is being said, and his concentration fractures whenever he is trying to monitor the room. At work this has become painful: during pastoral meetings he sometimes realizes he has missed the thread of what someone is telling him because he was tracking movement in the doorway or the possibility that someone might touch him unexpectedly. The more he watches for danger, the more quickly he spots reminders of it, and ordinary noise or motion can take on the force of the past.

His efforts to manage this have, in his own mind, become further proof of personal failure. Because he keeps distracting himself and restricting how emotionally close he allows himself to be, he tells himself he deserves to suffer for what happened and for the ways he has disappointed others since. When he withdraws from his partner after being startled, he later judges himself as weak and unreliable; when he spends a whole meeting focused on where the exits are, he concludes that someone else would have coped better. Those judgments feed back into his vigilance. Feeling that he cannot depend on himself, he becomes even more careful about where he sits and how much of the world he lets in, and in that tightened state he is even more sensitive to shouting, to anything weapon-like, to the shock of unprepared touch.

What finally brought David to seek help was a recent Sabbath morning when a teenage congregant came up from behind to hug him in thanks after a service. David jerked away so abruptly that the boy looked frightened. He spent the rest of the day distracted and ashamed, certain that his own reactions had made him unsafe to others as well as to himself. At home that night, when his partner tried to comfort him, he pulled back again. He says he is afraid that his world will continue shrinking until only a few places feel tolerable, and that he will become a man who can preach refuge to others while unable to find any himself. He is hoping, cautiously, to learn whether his body can stop living in the old emergency, and whether closeness can feel possible without danger.
